blocks.body:
Six students record how many hours they revised and the mark they got. Plotted as points, the data rise from left to right, roughly along a line. Two questions follow. How strong is the straight-line pattern? And which line describes it best, so that we can predict the mark of someone who revised for 7 hours?

Correlation answers the first question with a single number; least-squares regression answers the second with a formula. Both use the means and spreads of [[descriptive-statistics]], and the line is the simplest instance of the [[least-squares]] fitting of linear algebra.

blocks.title: Scatterplots and the sums S
blocks.body:
Start with a picture. A scatterplot shows each pair $(x_i, y_i)$ as a point, with the explanatory variable $x$ across and the response $y$ up. Describe it by direction (positive or negative), form (straight or curved), strength (tight or loose) and unusual points.

To measure a straight-line pattern, move the origin to the point of means $(\bar x,\bar y)$. A point up and to the right of it, or down and to the left, has $(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y) > 0$; the other two quadrants give negative products. Adding them up gives
$$S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y),$$
which is large and positive for a rising pattern and large and negative for a falling one. We also need the corresponding sums for each variable alone, $S_{xx} = \sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$ and $S_{yy} = \sum(y_i-\bar y)^2$. Useful shortcuts for hand calculation are $S_{xy} = \sum x_iy_i - n\bar x\bar y$ and $S_{xx} = \sum x_i^2 - n\bar x^2$.

blocks.title: Correlation coefficient
blocks.body:
For paired data with $S_{xx}, S_{yy} > 0$, the (Pearson product-moment) correlation coefficient is
$$r = \frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}\,S_{yy}}}.$$
Equivalently, $r$ is the average product of the standardised values $z_x = (x-\bar x)/s_x$ and $z_y = (y-\bar y)/s_y$, with divisor $n-1$.

It has no units, does not change if either variable is rescaled by a positive factor or shifted, and is symmetric in $x$ and $y$. As shown below, $-1 \le r \le 1$, with $r = \pm 1$ exactly when the points lie on a line.

blocks.title: Finding the best line
blocks.body: For a candidate line $\hat y = a + bx$, the residual of point $i$ is $e_i = y_i - (a+bx_i)$, the vertical distance from the point to the line. The least-squares line is the one making $\sum e_i^2$ as small as possible. Squaring treats points above and below alike and penalises large misses heavily; it also leads to formulas we can solve exactly.

blocks.title: The least-squares line
blocks.body:
Suppose $S_{xx} > 0$. Among all lines $\hat y = a+bx$, the sum of squared residuals is smallest exactly for
$$b = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \qquad a = \bar y - b\bar x,$$
and its minimum value is
$$\sum (y_i-\hat y_i)^2 = S_{yy} - \frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}} = (1-r^2)\,S_{yy}.$$
Consequently $r^2 \le 1$, with equality exactly when all points lie on one line.

First fix $b$ and vary $a$. The residuals are $e_i = (y_i - bx_i) - a$, and the sum of squared distances from numbers $w_i = y_i-bx_i$ to a constant $a$ is smallest when $a$ is their mean, since $\sum (w_i - a)^2 = \sum (w_i-\bar w)^2 + n(\bar w - a)^2$. So $a = \bar w = \bar y - b\bar x$; in particular the best line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$.

With this $a$, $e_i = (y_i-\bar y) - b(x_i-\bar x)$, and expanding the square,
$$\sum e_i^2 = S_{yy} - 2bS_{xy} + b^2S_{xx} = S_{xx}\Big(b - \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\Big)^2 + S_{yy} - \frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}},$$
by completing the square. This is smallest exactly when $b = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$, and the minimum is $S_{yy} - S_{xy}^2/S_{xx} = S_{yy}(1-r^2)$.

A sum of squares cannot be negative, so $1 - r^2 \ge 0$. It equals zero exactly when every residual is zero, that is when all points lie on the line.

blocks.title: Reading the line
blocks.body:
Three consequences of the theorem are worth knowing by heart.

1. The slope can be written $b = r\,s_y/s_x$. In standard units the line is simply $\hat z_y = r\,z_x$: a point one standard deviation above average in $x$ is predicted to be only $r$ standard deviations above average in $y$. When $|r|<1$ predictions are pulled towards the mean. This is regression to the mean, and it is where the word "regression" comes from: tall parents tend to have children who are tall, but on average less extreme.
2. The residuals add up to zero, and so do the residuals multiplied by $x_i$; these are the two equations that determine $a$ and $b$.
3. Since $S_{yy} = \sum(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2 + \sum e_i^2$, the quantity $r^2$ is the fraction of the variation in $y$ explained by the line, often written $R^2$ and called the coefficient of determination.

The slope has units (units of $y$ per unit of $x$) and is interpreted as the predicted change in $y$ for each extra unit of $x$. The intercept is the prediction at $x = 0$, which is meaningful only if $x = 0$ is within or near the range of the data.

blocks.title: Revision and marks
blocks.body:
A made-up sample of 6 students:
$$\begin{array}{c|cccccc} \text{hours } x & 2 & 3 & 5 & 6 & 8 & 10\\ \hline \text{mark } y & 55 & 60 & 64 & 70 & 76 & 85 \end{array}$$
Find $r$ and the least-squares line, predict the mark after 7 hours, and find the residual for the student who revised 5 hours.
blocks.solution:
The means are $\bar x = 34/6 = 17/3$ and $\bar y = 410/6 = 205/3$. Working with the deviations,
$$S_{xx} = \frac{136}{3} \approx 45.33,\qquad S_{yy} = \frac{1816}{3} \approx 605.33,\qquad S_{xy} = \frac{494}{3} \approx 164.67.$$
Then
$$r = \frac{494}{\sqrt{136\times 1816}} \approx 0.994,\qquad b = \frac{494}{136} \approx 3.632,\qquad a = \frac{205}{3} - \frac{494}{136}\cdot\frac{17}{3} = 47.75.$$
The line is $\hat y = 47.75 + 3.632x$: each extra hour of revision goes with about 3.6 more marks. At $x = 7$, $\hat y \approx 73.2$. At $x = 5$, $\hat y \approx 65.91$, so the residual is $64 - 65.91 = -1.91$: that student scored about 2 marks below the line.

Here $r^2 \approx 0.988$, so the line accounts for almost 99% of the variation in marks. As a check, the sum of squared residuals is $(1-r^2)S_{yy} \approx 7.21$. Of course this says nothing about whether revision causes higher marks; see the pitfalls.

blocks.title: Residual plots and curved data
blocks.body:
A high $r$ does not prove that a line is the right model. Plot the residuals $e_i$ against $x_i$. If the line is appropriate, they scatter randomly around zero with roughly constant spread. A curved pattern means the relationship is not linear; a fan shape means the spread changes with $x$.

When the pattern is curved, a transformation may straighten it. If $y$ grows exponentially, $y = Ce^{kx}$, then $\ln y = \ln C + kx$ is linear in $x$, so we regress $\ln y$ on $x$. A power law $y = Cx^p$ becomes linear after taking logarithms of both variables.

blocks.title: Fitting an exponential model
blocks.body:
A made-up bacteria culture is counted every hour:
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} t & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4\\ \hline N & 200 & 330 & 530 & 890 & 1450 \end{array}$$
Fit a model $N = Ce^{kt}$.
blocks.solution:
Regress $\ln N$ on $t$. The values of $\ln N$ are about $5.298, 5.799, 6.273, 6.791, 7.279$, and the least-squares line is
$$\widehat{\ln N} \approx 5.297 + 0.4954\,t,$$
with correlation $0.99993$. Exponentiating, $C \approx e^{5.297} \approx 199.8$ and $e^{k} \approx 1.641$, so $N \approx 199.8\,(1.641)^t$: the population grows by about 64% per hour. Plotting the residuals against $t$ for a straight line fitted to the raw counts would show a clear curve, which is the signal to transform.

blocks.title: Two regression lines
blocks.body: The line for predicting $y$ from $x$ minimises vertical residuals; the line for predicting $x$ from $y$ minimises horizontal ones. Show that both pass through $(\bar x,\bar y)$, that if the second is written $x = a' + b'y$ then $bb' = r^2$, and that the two lines coincide only when $r = \pm 1$.
blocks.solution:
By the theorem with the roles of the variables swapped, $b' = S_{xy}/S_{yy}$ and the line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$. Hence
$$bb' = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\cdot\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{yy}} = r^2.$$
In the $xy$-plane the second line has slope $1/b'$ (if $r \neq 0$). Both lines pass through the same point, so they coincide exactly when the slopes agree, $b = 1/b'$, that is $bb' = 1$, i.e. $r^2 = 1$. If $r = 0$, the first line is horizontal and the second is vertical. For $0<|r|<1$ the steeper of the two is always the $x$-on-$y$ line, and the angle between them closes as $|r|\to 1$. So "the line of best fit" depends on which variable you are trying to predict.

blocks.title: Ranks, and inference about the slope
blocks.body:
When the relationship is monotonic but not linear, or the data are rankings, use Spearman's rank correlation: replace each variable by its ranks and compute $r$ for the ranks. With no ties this simplifies to
$$r_s = 1 - \frac{6\sum d_i^2}{n(n^2-1)},$$
where $d_i$ is the difference between the two ranks of item $i$. Two judges ranking five entries as $1,2,3,4,5$ and $2,1,4,3,5$ give $\sum d_i^2 = 4$ and $r_s = 1 - 24/120 = 0.8$.

If the data come from a model $Y_i = \alpha + \beta x_i + \varepsilon_i$ with independent $N(0,\sigma^2)$ errors, the least-squares slope $b$ is an unbiased estimate of $\beta$ (it is also the maximum likelihood estimate, see [[point-estimation]]). Its standard error is $s/\sqrt{S_{xx}}$ with $s^2 = \sum e_i^2/(n-2)$, and $(b-\beta)/\text{SE}$ has the $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom; two degrees of freedom are used by the two fitted coefficients. For the revision data $s^2 \approx 7.206/4$, the standard error is about $0.199$, and the test of $\beta = 0$ gives $t \approx 18.2$ on 4 degrees of freedom, as in [[t-tests]].

blocks.title: The linear algebra view
blocks.body:
Put the data in vectors $\mathbf y = (y_1,\dots,y_n)$ and $\mathbf x = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$, and let $\mathbf 1$ be the all-ones vector. Fitting $a\mathbf 1 + b\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$ by least squares means finding the point of the plane spanned by $\mathbf 1$ and $\mathbf x$ closest to $\mathbf y$: the orthogonal projection. With the design matrix $X = [\mathbf 1\ \mathbf x]$ it solves the normal equations
$$X^{\mathsf T}X\begin{pmatrix} a\\ b\end{pmatrix} = X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y,$$
whose two rows are exactly "residuals sum to zero" and "residuals times $x$ sum to zero". The decomposition $S_{yy} = \sum(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2 + \sum e_i^2$ is Pythagoras' theorem for this projection.

Correlation is a cosine: for the centred vectors $\mathbf u = \mathbf x - \bar x\mathbf 1$ and $\mathbf v = \mathbf y - \bar y\mathbf 1$, $r = \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v/(|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|)$, so $|r| \le 1$ is the [[cauchy-schwarz]] inequality. With several explanatory variables the same matrix equation gives multiple regression.

- Correlation is not causation. Revision and marks may both be driven by motivation; ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. Only a randomised experiment ([[sampling-design]]) supports a causal claim.
- $r$ measures only straight-line association. A perfect parabola $y = x^2$ on $x = -2,\dots,2$ has $r = 0$. Always look at the scatterplot.
- Outliers and influential points (extreme in $x$) can change $r$ and the line dramatically.
- Extrapolating beyond the range of the data is unreliable: the revision line predicts more than 100 marks after 15 hours.
- Do not use the $y$-on-$x$ line to predict $x$ from $y$; use the other line.
- A correlation computed from averages (for example, of whole countries) is usually much stronger than the correlation for individuals.

Regression is the projection theorem of [[least-squares]] applied to data, and its solution is computed in practice by QR or [[svd]]. Inference for the slope uses [[t-tests]], and the normal-error model connects the least-squares line to maximum likelihood in [[point-estimation]]. Large models with millions of coefficients are fitted by [[gradient-descent]] on the same squared-error objective.

1. For the points $(1,2), (2,3), (3,5), (4,4), (5,6)$, compute $r$ and the least-squares line.
2. Show that the residuals of a least-squares line always sum to zero.
3. If every $x_i$ is converted from hours to minutes, what happens to $r$, to $b$ and to $a$?
4. Give five points with $r = 0$ for which $y$ is nevertheless completely determined by $x$.
